wanga-kingdom.t: The only centralised kingdom among the Luhya of western Kenya, whose king Mumia became a key ally of British colonial expansion.
wanga-kingdom.o: Wanga traditions say the kingdom was founded around the mid-17th century by Wanga, a prince who had migrated from the area of Tiriki or further west and established a royal line among the Luhya of the Mumias area. The capital lay at Elureko, near today's Mumias.
wanga-kingdom.r: The nabongo (king) ruled with clan elders and a royal council over a farming people, and used alliances with Maasai and Kalenjin warriors to raid and dominate neighbours. In the 19th century Swahili and Arab caravans used Wanga as a base. Nabongo Mumia (r. 1882 to 1949) welcomed the Imperial British East Africa Company and helped British expansion across western Kenya.
wanga-kingdom.e: The British made Mumia paramount chief of much of western Kenya, but in 1926 his authority was reduced to an honorary position, ending Wanga's role as a governing kingdom. The town of Mumias bears his name, and the title of nabongo survives as a cultural office.

western-yan.t: A wandering Murong Xianbei state born in the Former Qin collapse, which sacked Chang'an and then settled in Shanxi until Later Yan destroyed it in 394.
western-yan.o: After Former Qin's defeat at the Fei River in 383, Murong Hong, a prince of the deposed Former Yan house, rebelled in 384 near Chang'an, where many Xianbei had been resettled. His brother Murong Chong took over, captured and plundered Chang'an in 385 and proclaimed himself emperor.
western-yan.r: Western Yan was less a settled state than a migrating host of Xianbei soldiers and families, longing to return east. Its leaders were murdered in quick succession by their own followers. In 386 the host moved into Shanxi, where Murong Yong established himself at Changzi.
western-yan.e: Murong Yong refused to submit to his relative Murong Chui of Later Yan, who regarded himself as the rightful heir of the Yan line. In 394 Murong Chui invaded, took Changzi and executed Murong Yong.

western-chagatai-khanate.t: The Transoxianan half of the divided Chagatai Khanate, ruled in practice by Turkic amirs and the springboard for Timur's rise.
western-chagatai-khanate.o: The Chagatai Khanate split in the 1340s. In the west, the Qara'unas amir Qazaghan defeated and killed Khan Qazan in 1346 or 1347, after which Transoxiana was governed by amirs who set up puppet khans of Chagatai or Ögedei descent, while the east became Moghulistan.
western-chagatai-khanate.r: Real power lay with the Turkic and Mongol tribal amirs of the Barlas, Jalayir, Arlat and Qara'unas, who had settled among the towns of Transoxiana and adopted Islam. Qazaghan ruled as amir until his murder in 1358, after which rival amirs fought for control. The region was invaded twice by Tughlugh Timur of Moghulistan, in 1360 and 1361.
western-chagatai-khanate.e: Out of these struggles rose Timur of the Barlas, first allied with and then against Amir Husayn, Qazaghan's grandson. In 1370 Timur defeated Husayn at Balkh and took power, ruling through a puppet Chagatai khan and founding the Timurid Empire.

wanaparthy-samasthan.t: A Telugu-country estate of the Reddy Rajas of Wanaparthy, one of the leading samasthans holding land under the Nizams of Hyderabad.
wanaparthy-samasthan.o: The Rajas of Wanaparthy, of the Janampally family, established themselves in the region south of Hyderabad in the early 16th century; the register's date follows family tradition. They later held their estate as a samasthan, a tributary chiefship within Hyderabad State.
wanaparthy-samasthan.r: The Rajas paid tribute to the Nizam but ran their own revenue and courts. Successive rulers took the name Rameshwar Rao and supported Telugu and Sanskrit learning. They built the palace at Wanaparthy, later used as a college.
wanaparthy-samasthan.e: After Hyderabad was integrated into India in 1948, the samasthan's powers ended. The family's J. Rameshwar Rao later served as a member of the Indian Parliament. Wanaparthy is now a district of Telangana.

wabanaki-confederacy.t: An alliance of Algonquian peoples of northern New England and the Maritimes, the People of the Dawnland, long allied with New France against the English.
wabanaki-confederacy.o: The Abenaki, Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, Maliseet and Mi'kmaq shared related languages and ties of kinship and trade. In the later 17th century, facing Mohawk raids and English expansion after King Philip's War, they formalised an alliance, often dated to around 1680, with a council fire linked to the Catholic mission villages of the St Lawrence.
wabanaki-confederacy.r: Each nation kept its own sachems and territories, while the confederacy coordinated diplomacy and war through councils and wampum. Hunting, fishing, gathering and some maize farming supported communities from the Merrimack to Cape Breton. Allied with New France and supported by missionaries such as Sébastien Rale, the Wabanaki fought the English in a series of wars from 1688, including Father Rale's War in 1722 to 1725. Leaders such as the Penobscot sachem Madockawando dealt with both empires.
wabanaki-confederacy.e: After the fall of New France the nations signed Peace and Friendship Treaties with Britain. The confederacy gradually lapsed and was formally dissolved in 1862, but it was revived in 1993.

western-chalukya-empire.t: The Deccan empire of the Chalukyas of Kalyani, rival of the Cholas, whose reign saw a golden age of Kannada literature and ornate temple building.
western-chalukya-empire.o: In 973 Tailapa II, a feudatory of the Rashtrakuta dynasty claiming descent from the Chalukyas of Badami, overthrew Karka II and restored Chalukya rule over the western Deccan. He defeated the Paramara king Vakpati Munja, and his successors fought a long war with the Chola Empire for the Raichur doab and Vengi.
western-chalukya-empire.r: Someshvara I made Kalyani, modern Basavakalyan, the capital. Vikramaditya VI, who ruled from 1076 to 1126, started a new era and was celebrated in Bilhana's Sanskrit biography; the jurist Vijnaneshvara wrote the Mitakshara, a commentary on Hindu law, at his court. The empire's ornate temples, at Lakkundi, Itagi and Gadag, and its Kannada literature mark a creative peak, supported by trading guilds such as the Ainnurruvar.
western-chalukya-empire.e: In 1162 the Kalachuri minister Bijjala seized power, and during his rule the Lingayat reform of Basava began. Someshvara IV briefly restored the dynasty in 1184, but by 1189 its lands were divided between the Hoysala Empire and the Yadavas.

west-francia.t: Western third of the Carolingian realm, created at Verdun in 843, out of which the Kingdom of France grew.
west-francia.o: After civil war among the sons of Louis the Pious, the Treaty of Verdun in 843 gave Charles the Bald the lands west of the Scheldt, Meuse, Saône and Rhône. His realm took in Neustria, Aquitaine, Gascony and the Spanish March, though Brittany remained largely independent.
west-francia.r: Royal power weakened under the pressure of Viking raids and of great regional magnates who turned their offices into hereditary principalities. Charles the Bald ordered fortified bridges in the Edict of Pîtres in 864. Count Odo of Paris defended the city against the Vikings in 885 to 886 and was elected king, beginning a rivalry between Carolingians and his Robertian family.
west-francia.e: In 911 Charles the Simple granted Rollo the land that became the Duchy of Normandy. Kings alternated between the two families until the last Carolingian, Louis V, died in 987, when the magnates elected Hugh Capet, founding the Kingdom of France.

wari-empire.t: The first expansionist state of the Andean highlands, which built a network of administrative centres and roads across Peru centuries before the Incas.
wari-empire.o: Wari arose around 600 CE in the Ayacucho basin of the central Peruvian highlands, drawing on the local Huarpa culture and religious imagery shared with Tiwanaku. Its capital, Wari, grew into a city of perhaps 40,000 people covering several square kilometres.
wari-empire.r: From its capital Wari established planned provincial centres such as Pikillacta near Cusco, Viracochapampa in the north and Cerro Baúl in Moquegua, facing Tiwanaku. These rectangular compounds suggest a centralised administration that controlled labour and goods. Wari built terraces and roads that the Incas later reused, and may have used early khipus for records. Its tapestry tunics and colourful pottery spread a common style. Tombs at El Castillo de Huarmey show the wealth of Wari noblewomen.
wari-empire.e: The Wari state broke up around 1000, perhaps owing to drought and internal conflict, and its centres were abandoned. Its administrative model and roads influenced later states, notably the Inca Empire, while regional powers such as the Chanka Confederation and the Kingdom of Chimor rose in its wake.

western-satraps.t: Saka rulers of western India for nearly four centuries, whose king Rudradaman left the first long royal inscription in Sanskrit.
western-satraps.o: The Western Satraps were Saka governors who, under the Kushan Empire or independently, built a state in Gujarat, Malwa and Sindh in the 1st century. The first line, the Kshaharatas, reached its height under Nahapana. A second line, the Kardamakas, was founded by Chastana in Ujjain and became the main dynasty.
western-satraps.r: They controlled the rich port of Bharuch and the trade routes to Ujjain. Their silver coins, dated in the Saka era from 78, give an unusually exact chronology. Rudradaman I's Junagadh inscription of 150 boasts of his victories over the Satavahana dynasty and the Yaudheyas and of repairing the Sudarshana reservoir, and is written in elegant Sanskrit, a sign of its spread as a courtly language.
western-satraps.e: After long rivalry with the Satavahanas, the satraps declined in the 4th century. Around 395 to 415 the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II defeated the last ruler, Rudrasimha III, and annexed Gujarat and Malwa, opening the western ports to the Gupta Empire.

western-wei-206-bc.t: Wei Bao's kingdom in southern Shanxi, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms of 206 BCE, conquered by Han Xin's surprise crossing of the Yellow River.
western-wei-206-bc.o: Wei Bao, of the royal house of the old State of Wei, had been made King of Wei during the rising against the Qin dynasty. In Xiang Yu's settlement of 206 BCE he lost the Wei heartland around Daliang and was moved west to rule as King of Western Wei from Pingyang in the Fen valley of Shanxi.
western-wei-206-bc.r: The kingdom covered the Hedong region, rich in salt and grain, on the east bank of the Yellow River facing the Guanzhong region. It was a frontline state whose loyalty swung with the fortunes of Chu and Han.
western-wei-206-bc.e: Wei Bao joined Liu Bang in 205 BCE, then deserted him after the Han defeat at Pengcheng. That autumn Han Xin feinted at one ford while crossing at Xiayang on rafts of wooden jars, and captured Wei Bao. His concubine Bo Ji later bore Liu Bang a son, the future Emperor Wen of Han.

wang-jingwei-regime.t: The collaborationist government that the veteran Kuomintang leader Wang Jingwei set up at Nanjing in 1940 under Japanese protection.
wang-jingwei-regime.o: Wang Jingwei, a close associate of Sun Yat-sen and rival of Chiang Kai-shek, believed China could not win the war against Japan. He fled Chongqing in December 1938 and, after negotiations with Japan, inaugurated a 'reorganised' National Government at Nanjing on 30 March 1940, absorbing the Provisional Government of the Republic of China and the Reformed Government of the Republic of China.
wang-jingwei-regime.r: The regime used the name, flag and symbols of the Nationalist government, claiming to be its legitimate continuation. Japan recognised it in 1940, and in 1943 it declared war on Britain and the United States and took over the Shanghai International Settlement and the Shanghai French Concession. In practice Japanese armies controlled it, and Wang's officials, among them Chen Gongbo and Zhou Fohai, had limited room for action.
wang-jingwei-regime.e: Wang Jingwei died in Japan in November 1944, and Chen Gongbo succeeded him. The regime dissolved after Japan surrendered in August 1945. Its leaders were tried as traitors, and Chen Gongbo was executed in 1946.

water-chenla.t: The southern, lowland half of divided Chenla in the 8th century, a fragmented Khmer realm of the Mekong plains and delta.
water-chenla.o: After the death of Jayavarman I around 681, Chenla lost its unity, and Chinese records from about 707 distinguish a southern Water Chenla, Shui Zhenla, from Land Chenla. It covered the lower Mekong, the Tonle Sap region and the delta, the old lands of Funan.
water-chenla.r: Water Chenla appears to have been divided among several rulers, including a queen Jayadevi known from an inscription of 713 who complained of hard times. Centres such as Sambhupura, near Sambor on the Mekong, and Aninditapura held local power. Its kings followed Shaivite cults and wrote in Sanskrit and Old Khmer.
water-chenla.e: In the late 8th century Javanese raids, possibly from the Sailendra kingdom, struck the region. Jayavarman II, who had spent time in Java, returned to unite the Khmer lands and in 802 proclaimed himself universal monarch, ending the division and founding the Khmer Empire.

wusun.t: Nomads of the Ili valley and Issyk-Kul who became the Han dynasty's chief steppe ally against the Xiongnu, sealed by marriages to Chinese princesses.
wusun.o: The Wusun first lived near the Yuezhi in the Gansu region and were subject to the Xiongnu. Their ruler, the kunmo Liejiaomi, raised by the Xiongnu, led them west around 161 BCE to the Ili valley and the Issyk-Kul basin, driving out the Yuezhi and the Saka who had settled there.
wusun.r: The Han envoy Zhang Qian visited around 115 BCE seeking an alliance. The Wusun were pastoralists with large horse herds and, by Han count, some 630,000 people, ruled by the kunmo from the Red Valley city of Chigu. Han princesses, including Liu Xijun, who wrote a famous lament on her exile, married Wusun rulers, and in 71 BCE a joint Han-Wusun campaign struck the Xiongnu. A dual kingship of greater and lesser kunmo developed after 53 BCE.
wusun.e: The Wusun weakened through internal division and pressure from the Rouran Khaganate, moving into the Pamirs in the 5th century, after which they disappear as a distinct power. Their remnants merged into later Turkic peoples of the Zhetysu region.

wallis-and-futuna.t: A French Pacific territory of two island groups where three traditional kings still share authority with the French state.
wallis-and-futuna.o: Wallis was the seat of the Kingdom of Uvea, ruled by the Lavelua, and Futuna was divided between the kingdoms of Sigave and Alo. Marist missionaries arrived in 1837; on Futuna the priest Pierre Chanel was killed in 1841 and later canonised. Queen Amelia of Uvea signed a protectorate treaty with France in 1887, and the Futuna kings followed in 1888.
wallis-and-futuna.r: The protectorate was administered from New Caledonia, and the Catholic Church held great influence over schooling and daily life, while the kings kept customary authority over land and local justice. The islands lived by subsistence farming and fishing. During the Second World War Wallis hosted an American base. Many islanders emigrated to New Caledonia for work.
wallis-and-futuna.e: After a referendum in 1959, Wallis and Futuna became a French overseas territory in 1961 and an overseas collectivity in 2003. The three kings remain recognised in its statute, and more Wallisians and Futunans now live in New Caledonia than at home.

wild-and-rhinegraviate.t: A county on the Nahe and in the Hunsrück whose Wild- and Rhinegraves, ancestors of the princes of Salm, ruled from castles above Kirn.
wild-and-rhinegraviate.o: The Wildgraves held lands in the Hunsrück and on the Nahe, while the Rhinegraves ruled around Rheingrafenstein. In 1409 the Rhinegrave John III inherited the Wildgraviate, uniting both titles as Wild- and Rhinegraves. A marriage in 1475 later brought them half of the county of Salm in the Vosges.
wild-and-rhinegraviate.r: The family repeatedly divided its lands into branches such as Dhaun, Kyrburg and Grumbach, with Kyrburg castle above Kirn as a main seat. Most branches became Lutheran, though some Salm lines returned to Catholicism. The counts often served as officers in French and imperial armies, and branches were raised to princes as Salm-Salm and Salm-Kyrburg in the 17th and 18th centuries.
wild-and-rhinegraviate.e: French revolutionary armies occupied the left bank of the Rhine in 1794, ending the family's rule there. Compensated in 1803 with secularised lands in Westphalia, the princes of Salm formed the Principality of Salm, which France annexed in 1811.

wuyue.t: A peaceful and prosperous coastal kingdom around Hangzhou, famous for its Buddhist pagodas and sea trade, that handed itself over to the Song without a fight.
wuyue.o: Qian Liu, a former salt smuggler who became a soldier, defeated the rebel Dong Chang in 896 and gained control of the Zhejiang coast. In 907 the Later Liang named him Prince of Wuyue, and he governed from Qiantang (modern Hangzhou).
wuyue.r: The Qian rulers generally accepted the suzerainty of the northern dynasties, avoiding major wars except with their neighbour Wu (Ten Kingdoms) and its successor Southern Tang. They built sea walls along the Qiantang river, drained and irrigated land, and traded by sea with the Khitan, Korea and Japan. Wuyue was a great centre of Buddhism, and the Leifeng and Baochu pagodas of Hangzhou date from its rule.
wuyue.e: Qian Chu, the last king, helped the Song Dynasty conquer Southern Tang and in 978 surrendered his whole kingdom to Song without bloodshed. The Qian family was honoured at the Song court, and Hangzhou later became the Southern Song capital.

western-chu.t: The kingdom of Xiang Yu, Hegemon-King of Western Chu, who destroyed the Qin armies and redrew China's map, only to lose it all to Liu Bang at Gaixia in 202 BCE.
western-chu.o: Xiang Yu, grandson of the Chu general Xiang Yan, rose with his uncle Xiang Liang in the rebellion against the Qin dynasty. After his victory at Julu in 207 BCE he took Xianyang, killed the surrendered Qin ruler Ziying and burned the palaces. In 206 BCE he divided the empire into eighteen kingdoms and took for himself the title of Hegemon-King of Western Chu, ruling from Pengcheng (Xuzhou).
western-chu.r: Western Chu held nine commanderies of the old State of Chu and the State of Wei. Xiang Yu dominated the other kings by military force, but he alienated allies, had his nominal sovereign Emperor Yi of Chu killed in 205 BCE and treated defeated enemies brutally. His crushing victory over Liu Bang at Pengcheng was never turned into lasting advantage.
western-chu.e: Over four years of Chu-Han war, Liu Bang's alliances wore Western Chu down. Surrounded at Gaixia in 202 BCE and hearing Chu songs from the enemy camp, Xiang Yu broke out and killed himself by the Wu River. Liu Bang then founded the Han Dynasty.

wu-ten-kingdoms.t: The first of the southern Ten Kingdoms, ruled from Yangzhou by the Yang family and their powerful ministers, which became the basis of Southern Tang.
wu-ten-kingdoms.o: Yang Xingmi, a soldier of humble origins, won control of the Huainan region between the Huai and Yangtze rivers in the 890s and made Yangzhou his base. The Tang named him Prince of Wu in 902, and after the dynasty fell in 907 his family refused to recognise the Later Liang.
wu-ten-kingdoms.r: Wu was rich from salt production and Yangtze trade, and fought repeated wars with Wuyue and the northern dynasties. Yang Xingmi's sons were weak, and real power passed to the general Xu Wen and his adopted son Xu Zhigao, who ran the government from Jinling (Nanjing). Yang Pu took the title of emperor in 927.
wu-ten-kingdoms.e: In 937 Xu Zhigao made Yang Pu abdicate and founded his own dynasty, soon renamed Tang and known as Southern Tang, taking the name Li Bian. The Yang family was kept in confinement and later massacred.

wu-zhou.t: The Zhou dynasty proclaimed by Wu Zetian, the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own name, interrupting the Tang from 690 to 705.
wu-zhou.o: Wu Zhao, a concubine of Emperor Taizong, became empress to Emperor Gaozong in 655 and gradually took over government as he fell ill. After his death in 683 she deposed her son Zhongzong, kept Ruizong as a figurehead, crushed a Tang princes' revolt and in 690 proclaimed her own Zhou dynasty, with Luoyang, renamed Shendu, as capital.
wu-zhou.r: Wu Zetian promoted Buddhism, using the Great Cloud Sutra to support a female ruler, and favoured the Maitreya cult. She widened the examination system to recruit men from outside the old north-western aristocracy, invented new written characters and relied on informers and secret police such as Lai Junchen. The frontier wars against the Second Turkic Khaganate, Khitan and Tibetans had mixed results.
wu-zhou.e: In 705 ministers led by Zhang Jianzhi killed her favourites, the Zhang brothers, and forced the aged Wu Zetian to abdicate in favour of Zhongzong, restoring the Tang Dynasty. She died later that year and was buried with Gaozong at the Qianling mausoleum.

western-shu.t: A brief breakaway state in Sichuan, ruled by Qiao Zong after a mutiny of 405, which the Eastern Jin reconquered in 413.
western-shu.o: In 405 Eastern Jin troops in Sichuan, unwilling to campaign against Huan Xuan's surviving relatives, mutinied and killed their commander Mao Qu. They chose the officer Qiao Zong as leader, and he proclaimed himself Prince of Chengdu.
western-shu.r: Western Shu held the Chengdu plain and sought protection by accepting the overlordship of Later Qin, which recognised Qiao Zong as King of Shu. It also sheltered Huan clan fugitives and joined attacks on Eastern Jin territory along the Yangtze.
western-shu.e: In 412 Liu Yu sent Zhu Lingshi, who advanced by an unexpected route and captured Chengdu in 413. Qiao Zong fled and hanged himself, and Sichuan returned to the Eastern Jin.

warmians.t: Prussian people of Warmia, around the Vistula Lagoon, whose land became the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia after the Teutonic conquest.
warmians.o: The Warmians lived in Warmia, south-east of the Vistula Lagoon in today's northern Poland. They were one of the Prussian peoples recorded by Peter of Dusburg, with settlements along the Pasłęka and Łyna rivers.
warmians.r: Warmian society was led by nobles who held hillforts and controlled farming land, and its people kept the Prussian religion. The coast linked them to Baltic trade, including amber.
warmians.e: The Teutonic Order invaded in 1239, founding Balga castle, and soon dominated Warmia. During the Great Prussian Uprising the Warmians fought under their leader Glappe, who was captured and hanged at Königsberg. By 1274 they were subdued, and their land became the Bishopric of Warmia, a prince-bishopric that passed to Poland in 1466.

western-confederacy.t: An alliance of Native nations of the Great Lakes and Ohio country that resisted American expansion and inflicted the worst defeat ever suffered by the US Army against Native forces.
western-confederacy.o: The Treaty of Paris of 1783 gave the United States land north of the Ohio River that its Native inhabitants had never ceded. Building on earlier alliances, Shawnee, Miami, Lenape, Wyandot, Odawa, Ojibwe, Potawatomi and others coordinated through councils, with support from the Mohawk leader Joseph Brant, insisting on the Ohio as the boundary.
western-confederacy.r: The confederacy was a loose alliance of autonomous nations rather than a government, meeting in council and relying on war leaders such as Little Turtle of the Miami and Blue Jacket of the Shawnee. British posts at Detroit and elsewhere supplied arms. It defeated Josiah Harmar in 1790 and destroyed Arthur St. Clair's army on the Wabash in 1791.
western-confederacy.e: General Anthony Wayne defeated the alliance at Fallen Timbers in 1794, and the British refused shelter at Fort Miami. The Treaty of Greenville in 1795 ceded most of present-day Ohio. Resistance revived later in Tecumseh's Confederacy.

wambu-kingdom.t: An Ovimbundu kingdom of the central Angolan highlands whose lands became the site of the colonial city of Huambo.
wambu-kingdom.o: Wambu (Huambo) was one of the Ovimbundu kingdoms that emerged on the Benguela highlands by the 18th century, alongside the Bailundo Kingdom and the Viye Kingdom. Like its neighbours, it grew as a fortified raiding state with ruling lineages of mixed local and immigrant origin.
wambu-kingdom.r: Its kings ruled from hilltop fortresses through titled officials and village heads. Wambu's people farmed maize and beans and joined Ovimbundu long-distance caravans carrying slaves, ivory, beeswax and later rubber between the interior and Benguela. Detailed records of its rulers are scarce.
wambu-kingdom.e: Wambu was drawn into the Bailundo revolt of 1902 and occupied by Portuguese forces by 1902–03. In 1912 the Portuguese founded the city of Huambo on its lands, which became one of Angola's main cities.

wattasid-sultanate.t: The family of Marinid viziers who became sultans of Fez, ruling a shrunken Morocco squeezed between Portuguese enclaves and the rising Saadis.
wattasid-sultanate.o: The Banu Wattas, Zenata kin of the Marinids, governed Morocco as regents and viziers from 1420. After the last Marinid sultan was killed in Fez in 1465, a sharif ruled the city until Muhammad al-Shaykh al-Wattasi, who had just lost Arzila to Portugal in 1471, captured Fez in 1472 and proclaimed himself sultan.
wattasid-sultanate.r: Wattasid authority rarely reached far beyond Fez and the north. The Hintata emirate held Marrakesh, local lords ruled Chefchaouen and Tetouan, and the Kingdom of Portugal seized much of the Atlantic coast. The dynasty relied on truces with Portugal and the prestige of Fez's scholars, while Sufi brotherhoods led resistance to the Christians.
wattasid-sultanate.e: The Saadi Sultanate, leading holy war from the south, defeated the Wattasids and took Fez in 1549. Ali Abu Hassun briefly retook the city in 1554 with Ottoman help from the Regency of Algiers, but was killed the same year, ending the dynasty.

wuhuan.t: Nomads of the north-eastern frontier who served the Han as border guards and cavalry until Cao Cao crushed them at White Wolf Mountain in 207.
wuhuan.o: Like the Xianbei, the Wuhuan were survivors of the Donghu, who took refuge at the Wuhuan mountains after Modu of the Xiongnu destroyed them around 206 BCE. They lived in eastern Inner Mongolia and western Liaoning and paid tribute to the Xiongnu.
wuhuan.r: After the Han general Huo Qubing defeated the Xiongnu in 119 BCE, the Han Dynasty resettled Wuhuan bands along its frontier commanderies as guards and set up a Protector of the Wuhuan. They were herders and hunters ruled by elected chiefs, without a single king, and Wuhuan cavalry became famous mercenaries in Han wars.
wuhuan.e: In the late 2nd century Wuhuan chiefs such as Tadun allied with the warlord Yuan Shao. In 207 Cao Cao crossed the mountains and killed Tadun at White Wolf Mountain, then moved the Wuhuan into China, where their horsemen served his armies and they gradually merged with the Chinese and the Xianbei.

western-zhou.t: The dynasty that overthrew the Shang, introduced the idea of the Mandate of Heaven and ruled northern China through kinsmen planted across the land.
western-zhou.o: The Zhou were a people of the Wei River valley in Shaanxi who grew strong under King Wen. His son King Wu defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at Muye in 1046 BCE. After Wu's early death the Duke of Zhou acted as regent for the young King Cheng, crushed a rebellion of Shang loyalists and royal brothers, and built an eastern capital at Luoyi.
western-zhou.r: The kings ruled from Haojing and Fengjing near modern Xi'an and justified their power as the Mandate of Heaven, given to virtuous rulers and withdrawn from wicked ones. They granted lands to relatives and allies, who founded states such as the State of Lu, the State of Jin and the State of Yan. Long bronze inscriptions record appointments, gifts and lawsuits. In 841 BCE nobles expelled King Li, the first exactly dated year in Chinese history.
western-zhou.e: In 771 BCE the Marquis of Shen and the Quanrong sacked Haojing and killed King You. King Ping re-established the court at Luoyang, beginning the Eastern Zhou. Later Confucians idealised the early Western Zhou as China's golden age of ritual order.
western-zhou.re: Zhou ancestral religion and worship of Heaven

warri-kingdom.t: Itsekiri kingdom of the western Niger delta, founded by a Benin prince, whose kings adopted Catholicism and traded with Europe from the 16th century.
warri-kingdom.o: Itsekiri tradition holds that Ginuwa, a prince of the Benin Empire, left Benin around 1480 with followers and settled among the creeks of the western delta. His descendants took the title Olu, and the capital was established at Ode-Itsekiri, known to Europeans as Big Warri.
warri-kingdom.r: Warri's kings controlled trade between the interior and European ships. Portuguese missionaries converted the court, and around 1600 Olu Dom Domingos, educated in Portugal, married a Portuguese woman. Warri dealt in slaves, cloth and later palm oil. After the death of Olu Akengbuwa in 1848, rival houses could not agree on a successor and governors of the river held power.
warri-kingdom.e: The British signed a protection treaty in 1884 and in 1894 destroyed Ebrohimi, the town of the governor Nana Olomu. Warri became part of the Niger Coast Protectorate. The kingship was restored in 1936, and the Olu of Warri still reigns.

west-ukrainian-peoples-republic.t: The Ukrainian state of eastern Galicia, proclaimed in Lviv in 1918, which fought Poland and briefly united with the Ukrainian People's Republic.
west-ukrainian-peoples-republic.o: As the Austro-Hungarian Empire collapsed, Ukrainian soldiers seized Lviv on 1 November 1918, and a Ukrainian National Council proclaimed the West Ukrainian People's Republic over eastern Galicia, northern Bukovina and Transcarpathia. Yevhen Petrushevych became its president and Kost Levytsky headed the government.
west-ukrainian-peoples-republic.r: The republic quickly built a working administration, police and courts out of former Austrian institutions and formed the disciplined Ukrainian Galician Army. Polish residents of Lviv resisted, and the Polish-Ukrainian War began; the Ukrainians lost Lviv in November and moved the capital to Ternopil and then Stanislaviv. In January 1919 the republic proclaimed union with the Ukrainian People's Republic, keeping its own government.
west-ukrainian-peoples-republic.e: A Polish offensive in mid 1919 drove the Galician Army across the Zbruch in July, and the Second Polish Republic occupied the whole territory. Petrushevych's government went into exile, and the Allies recognised Polish rule over eastern Galicia in 1923.

western-xia.t: The empire of the Tangut people in north-west China, with its own script and Buddhist culture, destroyed by Genghis Khan in 1227.
western-xia.o: The Tanguts were a Tibeto-Burman people whose Tuoba chiefs governed the Xiazhou region in the Ordos as Tang and Song governors. Li Jiqian broke with the Song in 982, his son Li Deming expanded west into the Hexi Corridor, and in 1038 Li Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor of Great Xia, with his capital at Xingqing (modern Yinchuan).
western-xia.r: Western Xia combined a tribal military aristocracy with Chinese-style ministries. Li Yuanhao introduced a distinctive Tangut script in 1036, used for laws, histories and a huge translation of the Buddhist canon. The state controlled trade routes between China and Central Asia and fought the Song Dynasty, the Liao dynasty and the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), extracting subsidies from Song after 1044.
western-xia.e: The Mongols attacked from 1205. After Western Xia refused to join the campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire, Genghis Khan invaded in 1226; he died during the siege in 1227, and the capital fell soon after. The Tangut population was massacred or scattered.

witbooi-nama.t: The Nama community of Gibeon led by Hendrik Witbooi, the most persistent opponent of German colonial rule in Namibia.
witbooi-nama.o: The Witboois, or Khowesin, were an Oorlam group from the northern Cape. Around 1863 Kido Witbooi led them north from Pella to Gibeon in central southern Namibia, where a Rhenish mission was established and they became one of the leading Nama communities.
witbooi-nama.r: Hendrik Witbooi, grandson of Kido, saw himself as a Christian leader with a divine mission and fought long campaigns against the Herero for cattle and land. Literate and politically shrewd, he kept letters and a diary that are major sources. He refused German protection until a surprise German attack on his base at Hornkranz in 1893 forced him to submit in 1894.
witbooi-nama.e: Witbooi fought as a German ally for ten years, then rose against German South West Africa in October 1904. He was killed in 1905, and the Witbooi were deported, many dying on Shark Island; his image appears on Namibian banknotes.

wav-state.t: A small Chauhan Rajput state on the border of the Rann of Kutch in northern Gujarat, ruled by a Rana.
wav-state.o: Wav, or Vav, was held by Chauhan Rajputs who claimed descent from the medieval Chauhan rulers of Rajasthan. The register dates the state to around 1700. It lay in the desert fringe where Gujarat meets the Rann and Sind.
wav-state.r: The Rana ruled a dry territory of grazing land and millet fields. In the British period Wav was a minor state under the Palanpur and later the Banas Kantha Agency. Few further details are widely recorded.
wav-state.e: Wav merged into Bombay Province in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960, in Banaskantha district.

western-wei.t: The western half of the divided Northern Wei, controlled by Yuwen Tai, whose militia system and Guanlong elite laid the foundations of the Sui and Tang.
western-wei.o: Yuwen Tai, a general of Xianbei descent, controlled the Guanzhong region around Chang'an. When the Northern Wei emperor Xiaowu fled to him in 534, Yuwen Tai received him, then had him poisoned and in 535 installed Yuan Baoju as Emperor Wen of Western Wei.
western-wei.r: Western Wei was poorer and smaller than Eastern Wei, so Yuwen Tai built a new system. With the minister Su Chuo he issued administrative reforms, revived offices modelled on the Rites of Zhou and created the fubing militia, enrolling Chinese and Xianbei soldiers under Eight Pillars of State. This forged the Guanlong aristocracy. Western Wei took Sichuan in 553 and sacked the Liang dynasty's capital Jiangling in 554.
western-wei.e: Yuwen Tai died in 556, and in 557 his nephew Yuwen Hu had the last emperor abdicate to Yuwen Tai's son Yuwen Jue, founding the Northern Zhou. The Sui Dynasty and Tang Dynasty founders came from Western Wei's Guanlong elite.

western-kara-khanid-khanate.t: The western branch of the Kara-Khanid dynasty, ruling Samarkand and Bukhara under Seljuk and then Qara Khitai overlordship.
western-kara-khanid-khanate.o: When the Kara-Khanid Khanate divided around 1042, Ibrahim Tamghach Khan, son of Nasr ibn Ali, took Transoxiana and made Samarkand his capital, building a strong, centralised state that his descendants ruled.
western-kara-khanid-khanate.r: Ibrahim Tamghach Khan was remembered for justice, founding hospitals and madrasas in Samarkand. The khans ruled a settled Persian-speaking population with Turkic troops, and Bukhara was governed in time by the hereditary Burhan family of religious leaders. In 1089 the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah took Samarkand, making the khans vassals.
western-kara-khanid-khanate.e: After the Qara Khitai crushed the Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar at the Qatwan steppe in 1141, the khans became Qara Khitai vassals. The last khan, Uthman, was executed in 1212 by Muhammad II of the Khwarazmian Empire after a revolt in Samarkand.

wankaner-state.t: A Jhala Rajput state of Kathiawar on the Machhu river, known for its palaces and for rulers prominent in Indian public life.
wankaner-state.o: Wankaner was founded in 1605 by Sartanji, a member of the Jhala ruling house of Halvad (later Dhrangadhra State), who took lands on the Machhu river in northern Kathiawar.
wankaner-state.r: The Raj Sahebs ruled a territory of cotton and grain villages, paying tribute to the Gaekwads and Junagadh before British protection after 1807. Amarsinhji, who reigned from 1881 to 1948, built the Ranjit Vilas Palace and modernised the administration. It was an eleven-gun salute state.
wankaner-state.e: Wankaner merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960. Its royal family remained active in politics, and Digvijaysinhji served as a Union minister.

wahidi-sultanate.t: A coastal sultanate of the Wahidi tribe, centred on Balhaf, near the site of the ancient incense port of Qana.
wahidi-sultanate.o: The Wahidi tribe held the coast and hinterland between the Aulaqi lands and Hadramawt. The territory was divided among several branches, and the sultanate based at Balhaf emerged as a separate ruling line by around 1830.
wahidi-sultanate.r: The sultans ruled a coastal strip and valleys inland, living from fishing, farming and trade. Near Bir Ali in their territory lay the ruins of Qana, the main port of the ancient Kingdom of Hadramawt. The Wahidi sultanates signed treaties with Britain in the late 19th century and formed part of the Aden Protectorate. Balhaf joined the Federation of South Arabia in the early 1960s.
wahidi-sultanate.e: In 1967 the National Liberation Front took over the region and the sultanate was abolished and incorporated into South Yemen.

wadhwan-state.t: A Jhala Rajput state of Kathiawar on the Bhogavo river, one of the branches of the Halvad ruling house.
wadhwan-state.o: Wadhwan was founded in 1630 by a cadet of the Jhala house of Halvad, the line of Dhrangadhra State. The town had an older history as a medieval fortified centre.
wadhwan-state.r: The Thakore Sahibs ruled a territory of cotton villages, paying tribute to the Gaekwads before British protection after 1807. A British civil station grew up beside the town, later Surendranagar, and the railway made the area a cotton market. It was a nine-gun salute state.
wadhwan-state.e: Wadhwan merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960. Its old town is now part of Surendranagar.

western-qin.t: A Qifu Xianbei kingdom in Gansu that rose from the Former Qin collapse and survived among stronger neighbours for nearly half a century.
western-qin.o: The Qifu were a Xianbei clan settled around the upper Yellow River in Gansu. After Former Qin's collapse, Qifu Guoren declared himself ruler in 385, with his capital at Yuanchuan near modern Yuzhong.
western-qin.r: Western Qin was a small state of Xianbei herders and Chinese farmers, governed by tribal chiefs alongside Chinese officials. Qifu Gangui briefly submitted to Later Qin from 400 to 409 before restoring the state, which then conquered Southern Liang in 414. Buddhism flourished: an inscription of 420 in the Bingling Temple caves near the later capital Fuhan is the oldest dated one in a Chinese cave temple.
western-qin.e: Under attack from Northern Liang and Helian Xia, the last ruler, Qifu Mumo, tried to flee to Northern Wei but was captured by Helian Xia, which killed him and his clan in 431.

wehali.t: The ritual centre of central Timor, whose ruler was honoured as the source of authority by many Tetun and Bunak domains.
wehali.o: Wewiku-Wehali lay on the south coast of central Timor, in today's Malaka Regency. Its traditions place it at the origin of the land, the first dry ground to emerge from the sea. The register's start of 1500 reflects its appearance in Portuguese records of the 16th century, when sandalwood traders reached Timor.
wehali.r: Wehali was ruled by a sacred figure who remained still and inactive, while executive rulers called liurai governed and dealt with outsiders. Many domains across Timor acknowledged Wehali as their ritual elder. Society was matrilineal. Sandalwood and beeswax were traded to Portuguese, Chinese and Makassar merchants.
wehali.e: The Portuguese attacked Wehali in 1642, weakening its influence. Divided between Portuguese and Dutch spheres, its domains were brought under direct Dutch control by 1906. Wehali remains an important ritual centre in Indonesian West Timor.

wassa.t: An Akan kingdom on the goldfields of south-western Ghana, long squeezed between Denkyira, the Ashanti Empire and European forts on the coast.
wassa.o: Wassa emerged in the 17th century in the forest between the Pra and Ankobra rivers, a region rich in alluvial gold around Tarkwa. It was for a time subject to Denkyira, and after the collapse of Denkyira in 1701 it passed under the influence of the Ashanti Empire. The state later divided into two branches, Wassa Fiase and Wassa Amenfi.
wassa.r: Each branch was ruled by a king chosen from a royal matrilineage and advised by chiefs and elders, in the common Akan pattern. Gold mining and trading supplied the coastal forts of the Dutch Gold Coast and the British, and control of the paths to the sea gave Wassa some leverage. It repeatedly allied with the Fante and the British against Ashanti claims to the coast.
wassa.e: After the British victory over Ashanti in 1874, Wassa was absorbed into the new Gold Coast Colony. Its goldfields became the centre of the colonial mining industry from the 1870s, and the Wassa traditional areas survive within modern Ghana.

western-jin.t: The Sima family's dynasty that reunited China in 280 after the Three Kingdoms, only to tear itself apart in the War of the Eight Princes and lose the north.
western-jin.o: After decades in which the Sima family dominated Cao Wei, Sima Yan forced the last Wei emperor to abdicate in 266 and founded the Jin dynasty, ruling from Luoyang as Emperor Wu. Shu Han was already conquered, and in 280 Jin forces took Eastern Wu, reuniting China.
western-jin.r: Emperor Wu gave imperial princes their own armies and fiefs, demobilised provincial forces and introduced land allotment rules. The court and great families were famous for extravagance, and the Pure Conversation of philosophers like the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove flourished. Under Emperor Hui, who was mentally incapable, Empress Jia's intrigues triggered the War of the Eight Princes from 291 to 306.
western-jin.e: Exhausted by civil war, the dynasty could not resist risings by peoples settled inside the frontier. Han Zhao armies sacked Luoyang in 311 and took Chang'an in 316, capturing Emperor Min. A branch of the Sima family continued the dynasty in the south as the Eastern Jin.

wampanoag-confederacy.t: The alliance of Algonquian communities in south-eastern New England whose sachem Massasoit befriended the Plymouth Pilgrims and whose son Metacom led King Philip's War.
wampanoag-confederacy.o: The Wampanoag, People of the First Light, lived in some 60 or more communities across south-eastern Massachusetts, eastern Rhode Island, Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket. A devastating epidemic in 1616 to 1619 killed a large share of them shortly before the Pilgrims arrived, and the sachem Massasoit, ruling from Sowams, held the communities together.
wampanoag-confederacy.r: Local sachems governed their own villages but owed loyalty to the paramount sachem, who could call councils and warriors. People farmed maize and fished seasonally along the coast. In 1621 Massasoit made an alliance with Plymouth Colony, aided by the interpreter Tisquantum, and shared the harvest feast later called the first Thanksgiving. Missionaries such as John Eliot founded praying towns, and the Bible was printed in Wampanoag in 1663.
wampanoag-confederacy.e: English land hunger and pressure on Massasoit's sons Wamsutta and Metacom led to King Philip's War in 1675. Metacom was killed in 1676 and many captives were sold into slavery. The Mashpee and Aquinnah Wampanoag survive.

western-liang.t: A Chinese-ruled kingdom at Dunhuang, the westernmost of the Sixteen Kingdoms, whose founder Li Gao was later claimed as an ancestor by the Tang emperors.
western-liang.o: Li Gao, a Chinese official of the Longxi Li family, governed Dunhuang under Northern Liang. In 400 local officials proclaimed him Duke of Liang, and he broke away to rule the western Hexi Corridor, moving his capital from Dunhuang to Jiuquan in 405.
western-liang.r: Li Gao governed in the Confucian manner, encouraging schools, farming and irrigation, and acknowledged the Eastern Jin as his sovereign. Dunhuang, at the junction of the Silk Roads, was a centre of trade and Buddhist activity, and Western Liang preserved Chinese learning on the far frontier.
western-liang.e: Li Gao's son Li Xin was killed in battle with Northern Liang in 420; Juqu Mengxun then took Jiuquan, and in 421 he flooded Dunhuang and killed Li Xun. The Tang Dynasty's Li emperors traced their ancestry to Li Gao.

western-turkic-khaganate.t: The western half of the Turkic empire, which ruled the steppe from the Altai to the Volga and the oasis cities of Sogdiana and the Tarim.
western-turkic-khaganate.o: The First Turkic Khaganate, founded in 552 by Bumin, gave its western lands to his brother Istämi, who with Persia destroyed the Hephthalite Empire. Rivalries within the ruling Ashina clan led to a formal split around 603, when Tardu's successors ruled the west independently of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate.
western-turkic-khaganate.r: The khagans ruled from summer pastures and courts such as Suyab in the Chu valley over the 'On Oq', ten arrows or tribes in two wings. Sogdian merchants and scribes served them, and they sent embassies to Byzantium, allying with Heraclius against Persia in 627. Under Tong Yabghu, whom Xuanzang met in 630, the khaganate reached its height, collecting tribute from Sogdian cities and Tokharistan.
western-turkic-khaganate.e: After Tong Yabghu's murder, civil wars divided the tribes, and in 657 the Tang general Su Dingfang defeated the khagan Ashina Helu. The Ashina were installed as Tang puppets until about 742; power passed to the Turgesh Khaganate and the Karluk Yabgu.

witu-sultanate.t: A refuge state founded on the Kenyan mainland by the deposed rulers of Pate, briefly a German protectorate before passing to Britain.
witu-sultanate.o: In 1858 Ahmad ibn Fumo Bakari, called Simba, a member of the Nabhani family that had ruled the Pate Sultanate, fled from the Sultanate of Zanzibar's forces to the forests of the mainland and founded a new sultanate at Witu, north-west of Lamu. It drew runaway slaves and opponents of Zanzibar.
witu-sultanate.r: Witu was a small, fortified state of farmers and former slaves, ruled by the Nabhani sultan with Swahili notables. To protect himself from Zanzibar, Ahmad Simba accepted a German protectorate in 1885, negotiated by the Denhardt brothers, and the area was known as German Witu or Wituland.
witu-sultanate.e: Under the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty of 1890 Germany handed Witu to Britain. After Germans were killed there, a British force sacked the town in 1890 and Sultan Fumo Bakari fled. Witu was absorbed into the East Africa Protectorate, and the sultanate was formally ended in 1923.

wajo-kingdom.t: A Bugis kingdom of South Sulawesi with an elected ruler and a famous tradition of freedom, whose merchants traded across the archipelago.
wajo-kingdom.o: Wajo grew in the 15th century around Tosora on Lake Tempe, from a union of farming communities. Its chronicles describe a founding agreement between ruler and people that guaranteed the people's freedoms, summed up in the saying that the people of Wajo are free and only custom is their master.
wajo-kingdom.r: Wajo's head, the Arung Matoa, was elected by a council of lords and could be removed. La Tadampare Puang ri Ma'galatung, in the 16th century, is remembered as its wisest ruler. In 1582 Wajo joined Bone and Soppeng in the Tellumpoccoe, but in 1610 Gowa conquered it and imposed Islam. Wajo merchants built networks from Johor to Sumbawa.
wajo-kingdom.e: Wajo backed Gowa in the war of 1666 to 1669 and suffered when Gowa lost. In the 18th century La Maddukelleng returned from exile in Borneo to fight Bone and the Dutch. The Dutch conquered Wajo in 1906, and it is now a regency of South Sulawesi.

weimar-republic.t: Germany's first parliamentary democracy, born of defeat in 1918 and destroyed by depression and the rise of the Nazis.
weimar-republic.o: The German Empire collapsed in November 1918 with naval mutinies and revolution. On 9 November Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a republic in Berlin as William II abdicated. A national assembly met in Weimar to avoid unrest in the capital and adopted a democratic constitution in August 1919, with Friedrich Ebert as president.
weimar-republic.r: The republic faced the Treaty of Versailles, the Kapp Putsch, political murders and the hyperinflation of 1923, when the French occupied the Ruhr. Under Gustav Stresemann it stabilised, joined the League of Nations and saw a cultural flowering in Berlin, from the Bauhaus to cinema. The Great Depression brought mass unemployment and rule by emergency decree from 1930.
weimar-republic.e: President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933. The Reichstag fire decree and the Enabling Act of March 1933 destroyed parliamentary rule, ending the republic and beginning Nazi Germany.

western-guo.t: A Ji-clan state that moved from the Wei valley to the Yellow River, leaving the rich Guo cemetery at Sanmenxia, and fell to Jin in the famous ruse of the borrowed road.
western-guo.o: Western Guo was founded by a brother of King Wen of Zhou near Baoji in the Wei River valley. Around the end of the Western Zhou, its rulers moved east to Shangyang, near modern Sanmenxia in Henan, controlling a key crossing on the Yellow River.
western-guo.r: The dukes of Guo were senior ministers at the Zhou court and led royal campaigns into the 7th century BCE. The Shangcunling cemetery at Sanmenxia, with chariot pits and the tomb of Guo Ji containing jade burial garments and one of China's earliest iron-bladed swords, shows the state's wealth.
western-guo.e: In 655 BCE Duke Xian of Jin, having bribed the State of Yu to let his army pass, captured Shangyang and ended Guo, then destroyed Yu on the way home. The episode gave Chinese the idiom 'borrowing a road to destroy Guo'.

west-indies-federation.t: Britain's attempt to lead its Caribbean colonies to independence as one nation, which broke up after only four years when Jamaica voted to leave.
west-indies-federation.o: Discussions on federation began at Montego Bay in 1947. The West Indies Federation came into being on 3 January 1958, joining ten British territories: Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Leeward Islands of Antigua, Saint Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla and Montserrat, and the Windward Islands of Grenada, Saint Vincent, Saint Lucia and Dominica.
west-indies-federation.r: The federal government, led by Prime Minister Grantley Adams of Barbados with Lord Hailes as governor-general, sat in Port of Spain, as the chosen capital site at Chaguaramas was a US base. It had a small budget, no power over income tax and no customs union. Jamaica and Trinidad, the largest members, feared paying for the small islands and disagreed over free movement of people.
west-indies-federation.e: Jamaicans voted to leave in a referendum in September 1961, and Eric Williams declared that 'one from ten leaves nought'. The federation was dissolved on 31 May 1962. Shared institutions such as the University of the West Indies and the West Indies cricket team survived, and CARICOM later revived regional cooperation.

white-horde.t: The eastern wing of the Golden Horde, ruled by descendants of Jochi's son Orda on the steppes of Kazakhstan.
white-horde.o: After Jochi, Genghis Khan's eldest son, died in 1227, his lands were divided. His eldest son Orda received the eastern part, the left wing of the ulus, east of the Ural River, with its own line of khans subordinate to the Golden Horde. Names of the 'White' and 'Blue' wings are used inconsistently in the sources.
white-horde.r: The khans of the Orda line ruled nomadic Turkic and Mongol tribes in the steppes of the Syr Darya and the Irtysh, with towns such as Sighnaq and Sauran on the Syr Darya. The Orda khans enjoyed considerable autonomy and sent their own envoys to the Yuan and Ilkhanid courts.
white-horde.e: In the late 14th century the White Horde khan Tokhtamysh, backed by Timur, reunited it with the Golden Horde in 1378. After further civil wars the eastern lands passed to Shibanid and other Jochid princes, notably Abu'l-Khayr of the Uzbek Khanate in 1428.

white-croats.t: A shadowy Slavic people north of the Carpathians, named by a Byzantine emperor as the homeland of the Croats of the Adriatic.
white-croats.o: The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII wrote in the 10th century of a White or unbaptised Croatia beyond Hungary, from which some Croats had migrated to Dalmatia in the 7th century. Historians usually place the White Croats on the upper Dniester and Vistula, on both slopes of the Carpathians, but their exact territory is disputed.
white-croats.r: Very little is known of their society. They appear to have lived in fortified hill settlements, such as the large site at Stilsko near Lviv, and to have farmed and herded in the Carpathian foothills. The Primary Chronicle lists Croats among the East Slavic tribes who took part in Oleg's campaign against Constantinople in 907.
white-croats.e: In 992 Vladimir I of Kievan Rus' campaigned against the Croats, and they disappear from the sources soon afterwards. Their eastern lands became part of Rus' and later the Principality of Galicia, while the western parts around Krakow passed to the Duchy of Poland.

weihaiwei.t: A British naval leased territory on the Shandong coast, a quiet backwater ruled by scholar-commissioners until its return to China in 1930.
weihaiwei.o: In 1898, after Russia leased Port Arthur, Britain obtained Weihaiwei from the Qing Empire on a lease to last as long as Russia held Port Arthur. It served as a summer anchorage for the Royal Navy's China Station, with a base on Liugong island.
weihaiwei.r: After a brief military administration, a civil commissioner governed from Port Edward. The territory was never developed into a major port or base, and British rule was light, working through village headmen and Chinese custom. Its commissioners included the scholar-administrators James Stewart Lockhart and Reginald Johnston, former tutor to the last Qing emperor, Puyi.
weihaiwei.e: Britain agreed to return Weihaiwei at the Washington Conference of 1922, and it was handed to the Nationalist government on 1 October 1930, while the Royal Navy kept the use of Liugong island facilities for some years more.

wilusa.t: Wilusa, a kingdom of north-western Anatolia in Hittite texts, widely identified with Homer's Troy and its city of Ilios.
wilusa.o: Wilusa appears in Hittite records from the 15th century BCE, first as part of the Assuwa league. Most scholars identify it with Troy at Hisarlik, guarding the entrance to the Dardanelles, whose sixth and seventh cities were large walled citadels with a lower town.
wilusa.r: Its kings ruled as vassals of the Hittite Empire. Around 1280 BCE Muwatalli II made a treaty with Alaksandu of Wilusa, whose name resembles Alexandros, Homer's Paris, and the treaty invokes a god Appaliuna. Later letters show the Mycenaean king of Ahhiyawa contesting control of Wilusa and the deposition of a king named Walmu.
wilusa.e: Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire around 1180 BCE, at the end of the Late Bronze Age, and Wilusa vanishes from written sources. Greek epic transformed its memory into the story of the Trojan War.

western-liang-555-587.t: A small client state around Jiangling on the middle Yangtze, where a branch of the Liang imperial family reigned under Western Wei, Northern Zhou and Sui protection.
western-liang-555-587.o: In 554 Western Wei armies captured Jiangling and killed Emperor Yuan of Liang. The following year they installed his nephew Xiao Cha, a grandson of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and a rival of the Jiangling court, as emperor of a rump Liang state confined to the district around the city.
western-liang-555-587.r: Its emperors kept the full ceremony of a Chinese court, with reign titles and officials, but a Western Wei and later Northern Zhou garrison stood in Jiangling, and the rulers depended entirely on their northern patrons. The territory was only a few prefectures wide. Xiao Kui, the second emperor, was a respected scholar, and his daughter married Yang Guang, the future Emperor Yang of the Sui Dynasty.
western-liang-555-587.e: In 587 Emperor Wen of Sui summoned the third ruler, Xiao Cong, to Chang'an and abolished the state; some of its officials fled to the Chen dynasty. The Xiao family remained prominent under Sui and Tang thanks to the marriage tie.

west-jersey.t: A Quaker colony on the Delaware River whose 1677 Concessions and Agreements set out some of the most liberal rights of any 17th-century government.
west-jersey.o: In 1674 Lord Berkeley sold his half of New Jersey to the Quakers John Fenwick and Edward Byllynge, and William Penn became a trustee for the debt-ridden Byllynge. Fenwick founded Salem in 1675, and in 1677 a shipload of Quakers founded Burlington, which became the capital. The Quintipartite Deed of 1676 separated West Jersey from East Jersey.
west-jersey.r: The Concessions and Agreements of 1677, associated with Penn, guaranteed freedom of conscience, trial by jury and an elected assembly with wide powers. Quaker meetings shaped community life, and the colony served as a model for the Province of Pennsylvania. Farmers along the Delaware raised grain and livestock. After Byllynge's death the physician Daniel Coxe bought the governing rights in 1687 and sold them to the West Jersey Society in 1692.
west-jersey.e: Disputes between proprietors and settlers led to the surrender of government in 1702, reuniting West and East Jersey as the royal Province of New Jersey. The Council of Proprietors of West Jersey still meets in Burlington.

willoughbyland.t: An English sugar colony on the Suriname river, founded from Barbados, that was lost to the Dutch in 1667 in exchange for New York.
willoughbyland.o: In 1650 Francis, Lord Willoughby of Parham, the royalist governor of Barbados, sent Anthony Rowse with settlers to the Suriname river in Guiana. In 1652 Willoughby visited the colony, and in 1662 he received a royal grant from Charles II. The capital was Torarica, a small town on the river.
willoughbyland.r: Willoughbyland grew quickly to several thousand people, with some fifty sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Sephardic Jewish settlers, some from Dutch Brazil, were granted privileges and founded settlements along the river that later became Jodensavanne. The writer Aphra Behn claimed to have lived there and set her novel Oroonoko in the colony. A governor ruled with an assembly of planters.
willoughbyland.e: In 1667, during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, a Zeeland fleet under Abraham Crijnssen captured the colony. The Treaty of Breda that year confirmed Dutch possession of Suriname in exchange for England keeping New Netherland, renamed New York. Many English planters left by 1680.

west-breifne.t: The O'Rourke lordship of Leitrim, heir to the old kingdom of Breifne, which lasted until the Elizabethan and Jacobean conquest.
west-breifne.o: When the Kingdom of Breifne split in 1256, the O'Rourkes held the western part, roughly modern County Leitrim, while the O'Reillys took the east. Dromahair, by Lough Gill, became the O'Rourke seat.
west-breifne.r: West Breifne was a land of small lakes, hills and cattle-raising, ruled through Gaelic law with bardic and learned families. The O'Rourkes founded Creevelea Friary in 1508. Brian O'Rourke sheltered Spanish Armada survivors in 1588 and was executed at Tyburn in 1591 for treason.
west-breifne.e: His son Brian Og fought with O'Neill in the Nine Years' War. After defeat the lordship was shired as County Leitrim and, in the early 17th century, planted with English settlers within the Kingdom of Ireland.

warsangali-sultanate.t: A long-lived Somali sultanate on the Gulf of Aden coast, enriched by frankincense and later allied with the Dervish resistance.
warsangali-sultanate.o: According to tradition the Warsangali clan, of the Harti branch of the Darod, established a sultanate in the Sanaag region of northern Somalia around 1298 under the Gerad dynasty. Its centre was the coastal town of Las Khorey, with links inland to the highlands of the Cal Madow range.
warsangali-sultanate.r: The sultan, or gerad, ruled alongside clan elders according to Somali customary law and Islamic law. The economy rested on pastoralism and the export of frankincense, gum and livestock through Las Khorey to Aden and the Arabian coast. Like its neighbours, the sultanate was a clan polity rather than a centralised state, and its early history comes mostly from oral tradition.
warsangali-sultanate.e: In 1886 the sultanate signed a protection treaty with Britain and became part of British Somaliland. Sultan Mohamoud Ali Shire sided with the Dervish State and was exiled to the Seychelles in 1920. The sultan's title survives as a traditional office in the Sanaag region.

wassoulou-empire.t: The empire of Samori Toure, which fought French expansion in West Africa for nearly two decades with modern weapons and a disciplined army.
wassoulou-empire.o: Samori Toure, a Maninka trader turned soldier, built a following in the upper Niger region from the 1860s, conquering small chiefdoms in the Wassoulou and Konyan areas. By 1878 he ruled a substantial state with its capital at Bissandugu, and in 1884 he took the Muslim title almamy.
wassoulou-empire.r: Samori governed through provinces run by relatives and trusted commanders, with a standing army of sofa infantry. He bought repeating rifles in Freetown, paid for with gold, ivory and slaves, and had local smiths copy them. He promoted Islam and Qur'anic schools. After clashes from 1882 and treaties in 1886 and 1887, he fought the French repeatedly, and in the 1890s moved his whole state east, to the lands of the Kong Empire.
wassoulou-empire.e: In the east he destroyed Kong and fought the British and French. On 29 September 1898 the French captured him at Guelemou. Exiled to Gabon, he died in 1900, remembered across West Africa as a hero of resistance.

western-ganga-dynasty.t: The Ganga kings of southern Karnataka, great patrons of Jainism, whose minister raised the colossal statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola.
western-ganga-dynasty.o: The Western Gangas established themselves in the 4th century in Gangavadi, the southern Karnataka plateau, as the Pallava dynasty's power waned. Their early capital was Kolar, later moved to Talakad on the Kaveri. Tradition says the Jain teacher Simhanandi helped found the dynasty.
western-ganga-dynasty.r: Durvinita, an early king, was a scholar who translated works into Sanskrit. The Gangas often served as allies or feudatories of larger neighbours, the Chalukyas of Badami and the Rashtrakuta dynasty, and Butuga II fought for the Rashtrakutas against the Cholas. Their land grants supported Jain monasteries and Hindu temples. Around 983 Chavundaraya, minister of Rachamalla IV, commissioned the 17-metre statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola, and Kannada literature flourished.
western-ganga-dynasty.e: After the fall of the Rashtrakutas the Gangas lost their protector. Rajaraja I of the Chola Empire captured Talakad around 1000, ending Ganga rule; Gangavadi later passed to the Hoysala Empire.

wala-state.t: Kingdom of north-western Ghana centred on Wa, ruled by a Mole-Dagbani-linked dynasty alongside an influential Muslim community.
wala-state.o: Wala traditions describe the arrival in the 17th century of horsemen linked to the Dagbon and Mamprugu royal lines, who joined with Muslim Dyula traders and the local earth-priests to form a state around the town of Wa in the Black Volta region.
wala-state.r: The Wa Na was chosen in rotation from several royal gates, while Muslim families held important offices and the earth-priests kept control of land rites. Wa was a stage on routes linking the Niger bend with the Akan goldfields and Hausaland, and its Friday mosques reflect a long tradition of Islamic scholarship.
wala-state.e: In the 1880s and 1890s Wa was ravaged by the slave-raiding armies of Babatu and Samori Ture. Britain took control in the late 1890s, and Wa became part of the Northern Territories of the Gold Coast. The Wa Na still reigns.

waalo.t: Wolof kingdom at the mouth of the Senegal river, squeezed for two centuries between Moorish emirates and the French at Saint-Louis.
waalo.o: Waalo occupied the lower Senegal valley and delta. Wolof tradition makes it the home of Ndiadiane Ndiaye, the legendary founder of the Wolof political order, and the kingdom is dated to the late 13th century. For much of its early history it was a province of the Jolof Empire, ruled by a king titled the Brak.
waalo.r: The Brak was chosen from three royal maternal lineages by a council of electors, and the queen mother and royal women held real power. After Jolof broke up in 1549 Waalo was independent, trading slaves, gum arabic and grain with the French post at Saint-Louis, founded in 1659, while suffering raids from the Trarza emirate to the north.
waalo.e: In 1819 or 1820 Trarza and Moorish raiders attacked the royal town of Nder, where the women of the court chose death by fire rather than capture. Under Queen Ndatte Yalla resistance continued, but the French governor Faidherbe annexed Waalo in 1855 and it became part of French Senegal.
